other_side: Zitron would say the harness wars are a sideshow to a much larger dependency problem: it isn't enterprises who are dangerously reliant on OpenAI, it's the entire AI economy. By his arithmetic, OpenAI lost $20.9bn in 2025 on $13.07bn of revenue, carries over $800bn in compute obligations through 2030, and must raise on the order of $100bn or more essentially every year to survive — sums he argues no combination of SoftBank, private credit or an IPO can supply. Its spending is load-bearing for hyperscaler cloud revenue, neoclouds and chipmakers alike, so the question of which lab cuts off which coding tool matters far less than whether the lab writing the cheques 'runs out of money at some point'. Worrying about your harness vendor's whims, on his view, is planning the deckchairs.
truth_beneath: The single variable both men orbit is concentration risk — how dangerous it is to depend on one frontier lab. Both accept as fact that the labs cut off partners at will and that enterprises have organised themselves around a handful of providers. The empirical question that will resolve is whether OpenAI can keep funding its obligations: Zitron says it needs tens of billions within roughly three months, so watch whether a major raise or financing event lands by late November, and on what terms. The residue is pure worldview — whether the value being created ultimately justifies the spend. NLW is vindicated if enterprises that diversify models and harnesses ride out further cutoffs while the labs keep growing; Zitron if a funding crunch, not corporate pettiness, is what finally forces that diversification. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW sells strategic urgency, Zitron sells collapse — but note where they converge despite opposite priors: neither thinks you should depend on any one lab. That agreement is the signal. Next thing to watch: November 12th, when OpenAI's models go dark in Cursor, alongside any OpenAI raise announced before it.
editorial_note: Zitron published nothing on or after 2026-08-28 that addresses lab-vs-lab cutoffs directly; this Aug 18 piece is his most recent substantive statement on single-lab dependency, the edition's core theme.
